lead: A grid-tied converter links DC sources such as solar panels and batteries to the AC grid. It boosts the panel voltage, holds a DC bus, and inverts DC into sinusoidal current matched to the grid in phase, frequency and amplitude. The inverter controller sets power factor, harmonics, and power direction. This chapter covers the PV curve and maximum power point, hysteresis current control, real and reactive power from angle and voltage, and battery storage with its management system and converter.
prereq: You need Unit 4 (grid-tied inverters and PWM), Unit 3 (boost and bidirectional converters) and Unit 2 (power-factor-corrected rectifiers); 6.1 shows the same DC bus with a battery.

sections.h3: The PV curve and the maximum power point

blocks.text: A PV cell is a current source in parallel with a diode; sunlight sets the current. Short circuit: V = 0, I = Isc. Open circuit: I = 0, V = Voc. Power P = V × I, where V is terminal voltage in volts, I current in amperes, P power in watts. P is zero at both ends and peaks once in the knee: the maximum power point (MPP).
Irradiance moves current almost in proportion. Cell temperature moves voltage the other way, so a hot panel has lower Voc. The MPP slides all day, so the converter chases it.

Perturb and observe (P&O): measure V and I, compute P, step the boost duty, measure again, compare. If power rose, step same way; if it fell, reverse. It hunts around the MPP by one step but needs no panel model.

Two arrangements: two-stage has a boost MPPT stage onto a DC bus plus a separate inverter; single-stage lets the inverter do MPPT and accept a wider input window. Indian rooftop systems are mostly two-stage.

Hysteresis control makes inverter current follow a sine. Build reference iref(t) = Im sin(ωt) from grid phase and wanted power: Im is peak reference in amperes, ω = 2πf in rad/s, f grid frequency (50 Hz in India). Compare measured i with band of width h amperes: iref + h/2 and iref − h/2.

items: i climbs above iref + h/2: switch the leg so inductor voltage reverses and i falls.
i drops below iref − h/2: switch the other way and let i rise.
Repeat. The current stays in the band: a sine with small triangular ripple.

blocks.where: f_s is switching frequency in Hz; V_dc the DC bus voltage in volts; v_g the instantaneous grid voltage in volts; h the hysteresis band in amperes; L the filter inductance in henries. A full bridge is assumed.

blocks.text: The switching frequency varies: highest near v_g = 0, lowest near the sine peak. Design the filter at the lowest frequency. Switching loss is worst at the highest frequency, near v_g = 0. Conduction loss and device current stress peak near the sine peak because current is largest there. Direction comes from the sign of iref. Take current positive from converter into grid: a reference in phase with v_g exports real power (inversion); a reference 180° out of phase draws real power (rectification at unity power factor). The sign of the reference sets direction. One circuit charges and discharges a battery. Merits: fast, robust, no carrier, small steady-state error. Faults: swinging frequency complicates the filter and audible noise; loss varies through the cycle.

sections.h3: Real and reactive power from angle and voltage

blocks.text: Model the inverter as sinusoidal source E behind coupling reactance X feeding stiff grid V. E and V are rms phase voltages in volts, X in ohms mostly filter inductor, δ the angle by which E leads V.
P = (E V / X) sin δ        Q = (E V cos δ − V²) / X
blocks.where: P is real power per phase in watts; Q reactive power per phase in var; E the inverter fundamental phase voltage in volts; V the grid phase voltage in volts; X coupling reactance in ohms; δ load angle in radians.

blocks.text: Signs: δ > 0 gives P > 0, power leaves inverter (battery discharges or PV exports). δ < 0 gives P < 0, power enters (battery charges). For small δ, cos δ ≈ 1 and Q ≈ (E − V)V / X, so amplitude difference sets Q: E above V supplies reactive power, E below V absorbs it.

This turns a dispatch order such as “export 3 kW at unity power factor” into two references, δ and E. An outer loop sets them; an inner current loop, often hysteresis, forces current. Unity-power-factor rectification means δ slightly negative and E trimmed until Q = 0, that is E cos δ = V; current sits in phase with grid voltage and only real power is drawn.

sections.h3: Battery storage: cells, BMS and the power conversion system

items: Battery pack: cells in series and parallel give DC voltage and Ah. State of charge (SoC) is percentage capacity left; depth of discharge (DoD) is fraction used. Lead-acid is kept near 50% DoD; lithium goes deeper. A lithium pack returns roughly 90% of energy put in.

BMS: measures every cell voltage plus pack temperature and current, bleeds charge between cells, estimates SoC, and opens contactor on over-voltage, over-current or over-temperature. It protects cells; it does not control power.
PCS: bidirectional converter that charges and discharges to the DC bus. Charging is rectification at unity power factor; discharging is inversion under the P and Q rules above.

blocks.text: Grid services: peak shaving under time-of-day tariffs (charge at night, discharge into evening peak), backup during a power cut, frequency response and voltage support. A grid-tied inverter must detect a dead grid within a few cycles and stop, or it energises a line a lineman believes dead. Passive methods watch voltage and frequency windows; active methods inject a small disturbance and check whether it grows. Anti-islanding limits are fixed by IEEE 1547 and IEC 62116.

figure.caption: Power path from the panel to the grid. The battery reaches the same DC bus through a bidirectional converter, so the inverter is the only door to the grid and the hysteresis loop inside it sets both direction and power factor.

spec.title: Grid-tied PV with storage
spec.aria: A PV array feeds an MPPT boost stage, which holds a DC bus fed also by a battery through a bidirectional converter; a hysteresis-controlled inverter ties the bus to the grid.

examples.question: A home uses 4 kWh per day. The site gets 4.5 peak sun hours a day, the wiring and dust loss factor is 0.75, the inverter efficiency is 0.9, and the panels are rated 335 Wp. The battery is 48 V lithium, sized for 2 days of autonomy at 60% depth of discharge and 90% round-trip efficiency. Find the array size in Wp, the number of panels, the daily DC energy taken from the bus, and the battery Ah rating.
steps: The inverter is not lossless, so the DC bus must supply 4000 / 0.9 = 4444.4 Wh per day.
Array Wp = DC energy / (peak sun hours × loss factor) = 4444.4 / (4.5 × 0.75) = 4444.4 / 3.375 = 1316.9 Wp.
Panels = 1316.9 / 335 = 3.93, so round up to 4 panels, giving 4 × 335 = 1340 Wp. Daily DC from the array = 1340 × 4.5 × 0.75 = 4522.5 Wh, enough for 4444.4 Wh.
Energy to store = daily DC energy × days of autonomy / (DoD × round-trip efficiency) = 4444.4 × 2 / (0.6 × 0.9) = 16460.9 Wh.
Battery capacity = 16460.9 / 48 = 342.9 Ah; choose at least 350 Ah, or 400 Ah for margin. A 300 Ah block is below the requirement.
examples.answer: The array is 1316.9 Wp, rounded to 4 panels of 335 Wp (1340 Wp), and the battery is 342.9 Ah at 48 V, so choose 350 Ah or 400 Ah. A 300 Ah block is too small.
examples.check:
import math
E_day = 4000.0
psh = 4.5
loss = 0.75
eta_inv = 0.90
eta_rt = 0.90
panel_wp = 335.0
v_bat = 48.0
days = 2.0
dod = 0.60
dc_energy = E_day / eta_inv
array_wp = dc_energy / (psh * loss)
n = math.ceil(array_wp / panel_wp)
storage = dc_energy * days / (dod * eta_rt)
ah = storage / v_bat
print(round(array_wp, 1))
print(n)
print(round(dc_energy, 1))
print(round(storage, 1))
print(round(ah, 1))

traps: Sizing the array straight from kWh per day, forgetting peak sun hours and the loss factor.
Treating the battery Ah rating as usable energy — DoD, round-trip efficiency and inverter efficiency all apply and increase the size.
In P = (E V / X) sin δ, mixing line-to-line volts with per-phase X, or rms with peak; the formula is per phase and in rms.
Expecting fixed switching frequency from a hysteresis controller; band, inductance and bus voltage set the frequency.
Assuming a grid-tied inverter can keep running during a blackout — anti-islanding forces it to trip, so backup needs a separate battery inverter or transfer scheme.

quiz.q: What is the maximum power point of a PV panel?
quiz.a: The point on the I-V curve where V × I is largest; the MPPT steers boost duty to sit there.

quiz.q: Name the three layers of a battery energy storage system.
quiz.a: Battery pack, battery management system (BMS), power conversion system (PCS).

quiz.q: Why is hysteresis current controller switching frequency not constant?
quiz.a: Current crossing time depends on voltage across L: V_dc − v_g while rising and −V_dc − v_g while falling. Near the v_g peak net drive is small, current creeps, f_s falls.

quiz.q: A grid-tied inverter has E = 230 V per phase behind X = 2 Ω, feeding a 230 V grid at δ = 5°. Find real and reactive power per phase.
A rooftop inverter keeps exporting into a feeder the utility has switched off. Explain the danger and the missing function.
quiz.a: The inverter has islanded. The line stays live while a lineman expects it dead; the island has no earth reference and voltage and frequency drift, damaging loads; reconnection can be out of phase. Missing function: anti-islanding detection, passive or active, tripping within IEEE 1547 or IEC 62116 limits.

quiz.q: Why can one hysteresis-current circuit both charge and discharge a battery?
quiz.a: The loop only forces measured current to track the reference. Reversing the reference sign reverses power flow with the same switching logic and filter, so rectification and inversion need no extra hardware.

quiz.q: Give one reason for a two-stage PV converter over a single-stage one.
quiz.a: The boost stage decouples MPPT from the grid. The inverter input then sits at a fixed, higher bus voltage while panel voltage swings with temperature and irradiance.

beyond: Not for exam. Industry is moving from grid-following inverters, which need a stiff grid, to grid-forming inverters that set voltage and frequency and can run an island; search “grid-forming inverter” and “virtual synchronous machine”. Storage trials include second-life EV cells and flow batteries. Hybrid schemes pair a battery with a supercapacitor so the battery sees slow power. Green hydrogen uses the same DC bus to feed an electrolyser instead of the grid. Compare incremental-conductance MPPT with perturb-and-observe.
